blocks.text: “You know what a child I am. Why surprised?”

I did not want to answer that question in detail. But he begged me to, because he really wanted to know. So I explained what I thought, using the gentlest words I could. His behaviour seemed to show that he had ignored several duties to others. These were duties about right and wrong. This greatly amused and interested him. “No, really?” he said, with simple innocence.

“You know I don't pretend to be responsible. I never could manage that. Responsibility has always been above me—or below me,” said Mr. Skimpole. “I don't even know which. But my dear Miss Summerson explains this case so clearly. She always shows such good sense about everyday matters. If I understand her correctly, I would think this was mainly a question of money, do you know?”
Without being careful enough, I agreed that this was partly true.
“Ah! Then you see,” said Mr. Skimpole, shaking his head, “I have no hope of understanding it.”
As I stood up to leave, I suggested that he had done wrong. My guardian had trusted him, and he had broken that trust for money.
“My dear Miss Summerson,” he replied, with an open cheerfulness that was all his own. “I can't be bribed.”
“No,” he said. “Not by anybody. Money has no value to me. I don't care about it, I don't know about it, I don't want it, I don't keep it—it goes away from me at once. How can I be bribed?”
I showed that I disagreed, although I did not have the ability to argue about it.

“Quite the opposite,” said Mr. Skimpole. “In a case like that, I am exactly the man to put in a higher position. In a case like that, I am above the rest of mankind. In a case like that, I can act calmly and wisely. Fixed, unfair opinions do not twist me out of shape, as bandages do an Italian baby. I am as free as the air. I feel that I am as far beyond suspicion as Cæsar's wife.”
Surely nobody else had ever treated anything so lightly! He seemed to convince himself as he played with the question. He seemed fair to both sides, and tossed it about like a ball of feathers.

“Look at the case, my dear Miss Summerson. Here is a boy. He is taken into the house and put to bed. I strongly object to the state he is in. Once the boy is in bed, a man arrives—like the house that Jack built. Here is the man who demands the boy. The boy has been taken into the house and put to bed. I strongly object to the state he is in. Here is a bank-note offered by the man who demands the boy. The boy has been taken into the house and put to bed. I strongly object to the state he is in. Here is the Skimpole who accepts the bank-note offered by the man who demands the boy. The boy has been taken into the house and put to bed. I strongly object to the state he is in. Those are the facts. Very well. Should the Skimpole have refused the note? Why should the Skimpole have refused the note? Skimpole protests to Bucket: ‘What's this for? I don't understand it. It is of no use to me. Take it away.’ Bucket still begs Skimpole to accept it. Skimpole is not twisted by fixed, unfair opinions. Are there reasons why he should accept it? Yes. Skimpole sees them. What are they? Skimpole thinks to himself: this man is a tame lynx, an active police officer, an intelligent man. He puts his great energy into a particular kind of work. He is very clever at planning it and carrying it out. He finds our friends and enemies for us when they run away. He gets our property back when we are robbed. When we are murdered, he gets us our revenge without any trouble to us. Through his work, this active police officer and intelligent man has developed a strong belief in money. He finds it very useful himself, and makes it very useful to society. Should I weaken Bucket's belief because I do not have that belief myself? Should I deliberately make one of Bucket's weapons less sharp? Should I risk leaving Bucket unable to act when he next investigates a case? And there is another point. If Skimpole deserves blame for taking the note, Bucket deserves blame for offering it. Bucket deserves much more blame, because he is the man who understands these things. Now, Skimpole wishes to think well of Bucket. Skimpole believes that this matters, in its own small way. He must think well of Bucket to help keep things together as a whole. The government clearly asks him to trust Bucket. And he does. And that's all he does!”
